paragraphs: This paper asks how many relationships between tokens an attention layer can reliably represent with a fixed resource budget. It introduces a graph recognition task: attention must encode directed connections and recover the relevant neighbors when given only a subset of vertices. The budget is the combined key dimension across all attention heads.

Within a tractable model, the authors establish matching lower and upper capacity bounds, including explicit constructions. The required key dimension grows roughly with the number of relationships divided by the embedding dimension, apart from logarithmic factors. Splitting a fixed budget across multiple heads reduces interference between information superimposed in embeddings.

This provides a reason for multiple heads even when each query has just one target, rather than needing several kinds of targets. Controlled experiments show capacity transitions consistent with the theory. The advantage also survives increasingly realistic components, including softmax, value routing, and a full Transformer block using frozen GPT-2 embeddings.
icml-2026-a-capacity-based-rationale-for.tldr: Multiple attention heads can encode more relationships within a fixed key-dimension budget by reducing interference between embedded information.

paragraphs: Bilinear saddle-point problems describe interactions in which two players optimize opposing objectives. They appear in minimax learning, games, and constrained optimization. One way to help algorithms settle is to perturb the players’ payoffs. With symmetric perturbation, however, the perturbation must shrink to recover an equilibrium of the original problem, which slows convergence.

The paper instead perturbs only one player’s payoff. Its central result is that a sufficiently small asymmetric perturbation preserves an equilibrium strategy of the original game. This matters because the modified problem can support faster learning without requiring the same gradual reduction of perturbation strength.

Building on that result, the authors construct an algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence: the current strategy itself approaches equilibrium at a geometric rate. They also provide a parameter-free variant that retains this rate, addressing the need for a sufficiently small perturbation. Experiments demonstrate fast convergence in both normal-form and extensive-form games.
icml-2026-asymmetric-perturbation-in-sol.tldr: Perturbing only one player’s payoff enables fast equilibrium learning while preserving a solution of the original game.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good solutions when gradients are unavailable. Several established approaches solve this problem using seemingly different mechanisms. This paper places Evolution Strategies, Consensus-Based Optimization, Optimization via Integration, and related methods in a common framework, making their relationships explicit rather than treating them as separate algorithm families.

The framework identifies two main design choices. Fitness aggregation governs preference for sharper or flatter solutions, while consensus scope governs how the search handles multiple promising regions. These choices become adjustable ingredients for constructing hybrids. An Evolution Strategies–Integration hybrid explicitly controls the preference for flat minima, exposing a trade-off between performance and robustness.

Other hybrids combine the efficiency of parametric methods in higher dimensions with particle methods’ ability to represent multiple search regions. Evaluations cover standard optimization benchmarks, locomotion, and language model merging with limited evaluations. The hybrids can outperform their constituent methods, suggesting that understanding shared structure can directly guide useful algorithm design.
icml-2026-bridging-spherical-black-box-o.tldr: A shared framework for black-box optimizers reveals two design choices that enable effective hybrid algorithms.

paragraphs: CauSciBench examines whether language-model tools can carry out the full process of causal inference in scientific research. The central challenge is broader than writing working code: a system must choose an appropriate method, select variables, estimate causal effects, and interpret the statistical results in the context of the research question.

The benchmark includes more than 300 queries drawn from scientific publications, textbook exercises, established datasets, and synthetic scenarios. This range lets the authors assess performance across different kinds of research problems. Seven frontier models are evaluated on the pipeline, rather than judging their ability only through isolated programming tasks.

The models consistently perform worse on real datasets, and choosing the right causal inference method emerges as the main bottleneck. The finding locates a specific obstacle to automation: successful computation depends on first making suitable methodological choices. CauSciBench therefore measures research judgment alongside implementation, exposing failures that a coding-only evaluation would not directly target.
icml-2026-causcibench-can-llms-automate-.tldr: CauSciBench tests complete causal inference workflows and finds that selecting the right method is a major obstacle for frontier models.

paragraphs: Activation steering changes a language model’s behavior by adjusting its internal representations during inference. A common approach adds one direction everywhere, calculated from the average difference between contrasting examples. This paper argues that the approach becomes brittle when a concept occupies several context-dependent clusters rather than one uniform region.

The authors interpret steering as transporting representations from a source distribution to a target distribution. A single global shift corresponds to a restrictive case in which the distributions have the same shape and differ in their means. CHaRS relaxes this assumption by modeling both sides as Gaussian mixtures and computing transport between semantic clusters.

The resulting steering map depends on the input. It smoothly combines shifts associated with different clusters, so the intervention can vary with the representation’s location. Experiments across numerous settings show more effective behavioral control than global steering. The contribution is a structured way to make activation interventions responsive to how a concept is actually distributed.
icml-2026-concept-heterogeneity-aware-re.tldr: CHaRS steers language models with input-dependent combinations of cluster-level shifts instead of one global direction.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how language models internally represent sentence structure and meaning, focusing on DeepSeek-V3. The authors group sentences that share either syntax or semantics and average their hidden representation vectors. These averages, called centroids, capture a substantial portion of the corresponding linguistic information present in individual sentence representations.

To examine what the centroids contain, the authors subtract them from sentence vectors and measure changes in similarity. Removing a syntactic centroid strongly affects similarity to sentences with matching syntax; removing a semantic centroid affects similarity to sentences with matching meaning. This supports the idea that both kinds of information are at least partly encoded linearly.

The two signals also follow different patterns across the model’s layers and can be separated to some extent. Together, these findings suggest that syntax and meaning have distinguishable representational structure. The result is partial separation, rather than complete independence: simple vector operations expose meaningful components without establishing that all linguistic information fits this description.
icml-2026-differential-syntactic-and-sem.tldr: Sentence-vector averages reveal partially separable, partly linear encodings of syntax and meaning in DeepSeek-V3.

paragraphs: Human judgments can capture preferences that automated evaluation metrics miss, but evaluators differ in attention, expertise, and reliability. Asking people to compare two outputs improves consistency, yet those comparisons still need to be combined into overall scores. Treating every participant as equally reliable can distort the resulting ranking.

BBQ extends the Bradley-Terry comparison model with a Bayesian treatment that explicitly represents rater quality. It can reduce the influence of unreliable participants or remove them from consideration. Inference uses an expectation–maximization algorithm with a guarantee that the likelihood improves monotonically, providing a clearer optimization foundation than methods without convergence guarantees.

Experiments report efficient inference, well-calibrated uncertainty, and rankings that are more robust and interpretable than baseline Bradley-Terry models, including with noisy or crowdsourced evaluators. The practical value lies in extracting more dependable information from costly human comparisons. Modeling evaluator quality also makes uncertainty and disagreement part of the analysis rather than silently treating all votes alike.
icml-2026-efficient-bayesian-inference-f.tldr: BBQ improves rankings from pairwise human judgments by modeling rater reliability and providing calibrated uncertainty.

paragraphs: Predictive models can support lossless compression by assigning probabilities to upcoming symbols, which coding methods then use to represent a sequence efficiently. Powerful learned models can improve compression substantially. A practical complication is that identical models and inputs can produce different predictions on different machines, even when their parameters match.

Such differences matter because the encoder and decoder must interpret the compressed data consistently. Prediction mismatch can otherwise cause complete decoding failure. Probability Matching Interval Coding, or PMATIC, was introduced to tolerate bounded differences between their predictions, providing a way to use learned models despite this source of nondeterminism.

This paper generalizes PMATIC so that tighter theoretical results can shape the coding design and parameters can be optimized more flexibly. The authors report substantial improvements in compression efficiency and robustness. The contribution concerns the coding mechanism that makes model-based compression dependable: it improves how prediction disagreement is accommodated while retaining the benefits of probabilistic compression.
icml-2026-efficient-mismatch-tolerant-co.tldr: A generalized PMATIC coding framework improves compression efficiency and resilience to differences between encoder and decoder predictions.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models by training a smaller set of parameters. Even methods such as LoRA have adaptation memory requirements that grow with hidden dimension and rank. FrameFT addresses this remaining cost by representing weight updates through sparse coefficients in a mathematical construction called a Fusion Frame basis.

The basis can be generated algorithmically and shared across layers, while only its sparse coefficients are stored and optimized. This separates the structure used to express an update from the small set of values learned for a task. Sparsity in both the coefficients and the frames also provides computational benefits beyond reducing the trainable parameter count.

The paper supplies formal convergence results and evaluates supervised fine-tuning, primarily on language tasks, with applicability also reported for vision models. FrameFT matches or exceeds leading parameter-efficient methods while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and less memory. Its central contribution is a different representation of adaptation, designed to make the update itself cheaper to learn and retain.
icml-2026-fine-tuning-of-transformer-mod.tldr: FrameFT expresses weight updates with sparse coefficients in shared, algorithmically generated bases to reduce fine-tuning memory and computation.

paragraphs: Functional brain graphs describe weighted connections across brain regions. Researchers often summarize them with separate structural or spectral measurements, even though these measurements overlap and vary together. This paper starts from the expectation that dense brain graphs occupy a lower-dimensional geometry along which their properties change smoothly across a population.

The authors train a graph transformer autoencoder to produce compact representations of whole brain graphs. Aligned functional gradient geometry supplies domain-specific guidance for learning. This addresses two challenges identified in the paper: scarce labels for supervised training and the limited ability of node-focused embeddings to summarize an entire dense connectome.

Although training is fully unsupervised, the learned representations distinguish cognitive states and support decoding of visual stimuli. Adding neural dynamics improves performance further. The authors also train a diffusion model in the learned representation space and decode its samples into synthetic brain graphs. The representation therefore supports both analysis of observed connectomes and generation of new ones.
icml-2026-geometry-guided-generative-rep.tldr: A geometry-guided autoencoder learns compact brain-graph representations that support cognitive analysis and diffusion-based connectome generation.

paragraphs: Language models trained with rewards can exploit flaws in the reward signal and learn unintended behavior. A common response limits movement away from a reference model using a KL penalty. This paper instead asks whether training can favor regions where the reward itself remains a more accurate guide to desired behavior.

The authors derive a theoretical connection between reward-model accuracy and the flatness of the solution reached by training. They find an empirical relationship between gradient norm and reward accuracy, and show that resetting the KL reference leads to flatter regions with more accurate rewards. They then directly encourage this behavior using gradient regularization estimated efficiently through finite differences.

Across the reported reinforcement-learning experiments, gradient regularization outperforms a KL penalty. It improves GPT-judged preference outcomes, reduces excessive attention to formatting under rule-based mathematical rewards, and prevents judge exploitation in the evaluated mathematical tasks. These findings support shaping the training landscape as a way to mitigate reward hacking.
icml-2026-gradient-regularization-mitiga.tldr: Gradient regularization reduces reward hacking by steering language-model training toward flatter regions where rewards are more accurate.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions by penalizing violations of differential equations and auxiliary constraints. Standard squared-error training corresponds to treating residuals as independent Gaussian quantities with a shared fixed variance. This paper finds theoretically and empirically that training residuals instead vary substantially and have heavy tails, making extreme errors more influential than this model anticipates.

The authors replace the Gaussian residual model with a Student-t model. Its hierarchical formulation produces an expectation–maximization procedure that alternates between estimating weights for individual residuals and updating the network with weighted squared error. Existing PINN solvers can therefore handle the network-update step while the weighting changes how errors influence learning.

The resulting dynamics bound the influence of extreme residuals, preventing a few large errors from disproportionately controlling optimization. The method has almost sure convergence guarantees under standard stochastic optimization assumptions. Across challenging differential-equation benchmarks, it improves solution accuracy and robustness, connecting a better statistical description of residuals to more balanced training.
icml-2026-heavy-tailed-physics-informed-.tldr: Modeling PINN residuals with a Student-t distribution yields adaptive error weights that improve training accuracy and robustness.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to generate large visual-reasoning datasets beyond visual mathematics. The process first creates diverse, verifiable questions from existing images, then combines simpler questions into more complex compositional problems. The resulting collection contains over one million problems, including reasoning traces, preference examples, and instruction prompts.

These different data forms support supervised fine-tuning as well as offline and online reinforcement learning. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the evaluated open-data baselines, and the strongest configurations match or exceed strong closed-data models on several visual benchmarks. Training also improves text reasoning, audio reasoning, and embodied question answering despite the dataset’s exclusively visual focus and lack of embodied examples.

The authors use the dataset to study the broader post-training process. They find that high-quality supervised reasoning traces are essential for scaling online reinforcement learning, while offline reinforcement learning can match online performance with separated compute demands. High-quality supervised training also improves transfer beyond the training domain and modality.
icml-2026-long-grounded-thoughts-synthes.tldr: A million-plus synthetic visual-reasoning problems improve visual models and reveal benefits for reasoning across other modalities.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can improve performance on a target distribution while reducing robustness when inputs change. Averaging multiple fine-tuned checkpoints can soften this trade-off, but training and storing many models is expensive. MonoSoup aims to retain much of that benefit through a post-processing method using a single fine-tuned checkpoint, without additional data or hyperparameter tuning.

The method applies singular value decomposition to each layer’s weight update. It distinguishes high-energy directions associated with task adaptation from low-energy directions that introduce noise but may retain useful robustness signals. Rather than simply discarding the latter, MonoSoup automatically reweights the components using entropy-based effective rank and layer-specific spectral and geometric information.

Evaluations include CLIP models adapted to ImageNet and tested under natural distribution shifts, alongside Qwen models assessed on mathematical reasoning and multiple-choice tasks. The reported results show a practical balance between target-task performance and robustness. The approach makes the structure of one adaptation update serve a purpose otherwise addressed through multiple checkpoints.
icml-2026-model-soups-need-only-one-ingr.tldr: MonoSoup reweights a single model’s fine-tuning updates to retain adaptation gains while improving robustness under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Independently trained neural networks can develop similar internal representations, but comparing many models creates a coordination problem. Aligning every pair requires a number of mappings that grows quadratically with the model count and does not establish one consistent reference space. This paper studies a shared alignment for three or more models.

The authors adapt Generalized Procrustes Analysis to construct a common space using orthogonal transformations, which preserve each representation’s internal geometry. That preservation matters for applications such as connecting parts of different models. However, they find that insisting on distance-preserving alignment is suboptimal for retrieval, where methods that maximize agreement can perform better.

Geometry-Corrected Procrustes Alignment combines these priorities. It first builds a shared Procrustes-based reference space, then applies a correction for directional mismatch. Experiments show consistent improvements in retrieval between arbitrary model pairs while retaining a practical common reference. The result separates the task of establishing shared coordinates from the additional adjustment needed for effective retrieval.
icml-2026-multi-way-representation-align.tldr: GCPA aligns multiple models in one shared representation space and corrects directional mismatch to improve cross-model retrieval.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks incorporate physical equations into learning, but their predictions can still be inaccurate. This paper attributes important failures to two structural problems. Gradient shattering weakens useful training signals as depth increases, while flow mismatch sends predictions along update trajectories that diverge from the path toward the differential equation’s solution.

ResPINNs reorganize the network as a residual flow: successive stages explicitly correct the current prediction. This makes the architecture resemble an iterative numerical solver, with depth serving as a sequence of refinements. The design targets both the usefulness of the gradients and the direction in which predictions evolve during learning.

The analysis shows that these corrective steps preserve informative gradients across depth and keep updates aligned with descent. Experiments on partial differential equation benchmarks report higher accuracy with substantially fewer parameters than conventional architectures. The findings suggest that arranging computation around repeated correction can matter more than simply increasing network size when learning solutions constrained by physical laws.
icml-2026-physics-informed-residual-flow.tldr: ResPINNs use explicit prediction-refinement steps to improve gradient flow and solve differential equations more accurately with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Boosting combines multiple weak predictors into a stronger classifier. Each individual predictor needs to perform only slightly better than random guessing, but their combined votes can support reliable decisions. QuantumBoost focuses on reducing the computational cost of this process while retaining the goal of learning from weak hypotheses.

The algorithm combines two ideas. First, it uses a quantum procedure to accelerate approximate Bregman projections, an optimization operation used in its boosting process. Second, it applies a lazy projection strategy, performing these operations only intermittently instead of on every iteration. The savings therefore come from both making projections faster and needing them less frequently.

The authors report the best known runtime among boosting methods and identify their approach as the first successful use of lazy projections for boosting, whether classical or quantum. Its conceptual contribution is the combination: a scheduling idea from convex optimization works alongside a quantum computational improvement to accelerate the construction of a strong learner.
icml-2026-quantumboost-a-lazy-yet-fast-q.tldr: QuantumBoost accelerates boosting by combining faster quantum projections with a strategy that performs projections less often.

paragraphs: Large-scale language pretraining has enabled rapid adaptation to many tasks, but comparable flexibility remains difficult in vision. This paper investigates whether video diffusion models offer useful foundations for visual problem-solving. The motivating hypothesis is that learning from spatial and temporal data builds useful expectations about structure and dynamics.

The authors design a controlled evaluation comparing a pretrained language model with a pretrained video diffusion model. Both receive lightweight adapters, and tasks are presented in each model’s natural modality. The benchmark collection includes ARC-AGI, ConceptARC, visual games, route planning, and cellular automata, spanning several forms of structured visual reasoning.

Across these evaluations, video diffusion models show greater data efficiency than their language counterparts. This supports the hypothesis that video pretraining supplies useful structure for adapting to visual tasks with limited supervision. The finding concerns the tested adaptation setup and offers evidence for video pretraining as a direction toward more broadly useful visual foundation models.
icml-2026-rethinking-visual-intelligence.tldr: Video-pretrained diffusion models adapt more data-efficiently than language models across the evaluated visual reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Dynamic sparse training maintains a network with relatively few active connections while changing which connections are present during learning. This promises lower computation, but sparse models often converge more slowly than dense ones. As a result, reaching comparable accuracy can require similar overall training time despite the smaller active network.

This paper identifies Batch Normalization as a contributor to the problem. Through analytical and empirical work, the authors show that it adversely affects sparse training, highlighting an interaction between normalization, sparse layers, and changing network topology. They introduce SparseOpt, an optimizer designed to account for sparsity and address the resulting training difficulty.

Experiments with ResNet models on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet show consistently faster convergence and better generalization. The contribution is both diagnostic and practical: it identifies why a standard training component can undermine sparse computation, then changes optimization to respond. These results advance the goal of turning sparsity’s computational promise into useful training-time improvements.
icml-2026-sparseopt-addressing-normaliza.tldr: SparseOpt accounts for harmful interactions between Batch Normalization and sparse training to improve convergence and generalization.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation, but its benefit depends on the data being processed. A narrow workload can therefore give a misleading picture of speed. SPEED-Bench addresses this by evaluating the technique across diverse semantic domains and serving conditions, with explicit attention to both response latency and overall throughput.

The suite has two complementary splits. Its Qualitative split prioritizes semantic diversity, while its Throughput split supports different levels of concurrent demand, from small batches to heavy load. Integration with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM brings evaluation into production-oriented inference engines, exposing behavior that high-level implementations may obscure.

The benchmark demonstrates that synthetic inputs can overestimate real-world throughput and that the best draft length changes with batch size. It also identifies biases from low-diversity data and examines caveats of vocabulary pruning in advanced drafters. These findings show why a speculative-decoding comparison needs representative inputs and serving regimes rather than a single headline speedup.
icml-2026-speed-bench-a-unified-and-dive.tldr: SPEED-Bench evaluates speculative decoding with diverse inputs and realistic serving loads to reveal workload-dependent performance.

paragraphs: A training dataset can influence model behavior in ways that are not obvious from inspecting individual examples. This paper seeks a general mechanism for these hidden effects, motivated by the challenge they pose to understanding training through visible dataset content alone. Its approach draws on the linear structure of language-model representations.

The authors introduce Logit-Linear Selection, a method for choosing subsets of a generic preference dataset to induce particular hidden effects. Rather than requiring examples that openly state the target behavior, the method identifies collections whose training influence produces it. This makes subset selection itself a mechanism for shaping a model’s properties.

On real-world datasets, selected subsets induce specific preferences, changes in persona, and responses in a language absent from the dataset. The effects also persist across models with different architectures. That transfer supports the generality of the mechanism and shows why understanding a dataset’s behavioral influence requires attention to patterns across examples, not just their individually visible content.
icml-2026-subliminal-effects-in-your-dat.tldr: Logit-Linear Selection finds preference-data subsets that induce hidden behavioral changes across different model architectures.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization trains language models from preferred and dispreferred answers without reinforcement-learning rollouts. Its simplicity comes with a weakness: treating preferences as flat winner–loser labels can make training sensitive to noisy judgments or fragile reasoning. TUR-DPO adds information about how an answer is derived to the preference-learning process.

The method elicits lightweight representations of reasoning structure and combines their quality with semantic faithfulness and utility to estimate uncertainty. A small learnable reward is separated across these signals and incorporated into an uncertainty-weighted DPO objective. Training remains reinforcement-learning-free and uses a fixed or moving reference policy.

Across open 7–8B models, the authors report better judge win rates, faithfulness, and calibration than DPO on mathematics, factual questions, summarization, and dialogue. They also observe gains in multimodal and long-context settings. On reasoning-focused tasks, TUR-DPO matches or exceeds PPO, suggesting that richer preference signals can improve alignment while preserving a comparatively simple training procedure.
icml-2026-tur-dpo-topology-and-uncertain.tldr: TUR-DPO incorporates reasoning structure and uncertainty into preference training to improve alignment without online reinforcement-learning rollouts.

paragraphs: Activation steering adapts a model by changing internal activations, but choosing where and how to intervene often relies on experimentation. This paper derives a first-order relationship between activation changes and weight updates. It specifies conditions under which steering can reproduce fine-tuning behavior, giving these design choices a theoretical foundation.

The analysis identifies the output after a model block as an expressive intervention location. It also explains why different locations have different capabilities and why weight updates and activation changes can serve complementary functions. This motivates joint adaptation, which trains adjustments in both spaces together rather than relying on either alone.

Post-block steering reaches average accuracy within 0.2%–0.9% of full-parameter tuning while training only 0.04% of model parameters. It consistently outperforms the compared steering and parameter-efficient methods, including ReFT and LoRA. Joint adaptation often exceeds what either update type achieves separately, showing practical value in both the proposed intervention location and the complementary roles identified by the analysis.
icml-2026-weight-updates-as-activation-s.tldr: A first-order link between weight and activation updates guides efficient post-block steering and motivates stronger joint adaptation.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether knowing which outcomes players prefer is enough to predict where learning in a game will settle. It studies preference graphs alongside no-regret learning dynamics such as follow-the-regularized-leader. The distinction matters because preferences record the direction of improvement without recording how large each payoff improvement is.

The authors show that the pure strategy profiles within any dynamically stable set must be closed under profitable deviations: an improving move cannot lead outside that collection. For subgames formed by restricting each player’s available actions, preferences also characterize asymptotic stability. In this structured case, preference information provides the desired connection to long-run behavior.

The equivalence fails more generally. A constructed three-player game has a preferentially stable set whose span is dynamically unstable. To bridge the gap, the paper introduces resilience under aggregate deviations, an easily checked condition that uses payoff information and guarantees asymptotic stability for arbitrary spans. Preference ordering thus provides useful constraints but is not always sufficient.
icml-2026-what-preferences-canand-cannot.tldr: Preference graphs characterize learning stability in subgames, but more general stability requires additional payoff information.

paragraphs: Low-rank compression replaces large weight matrices with smaller factors, reducing storage and potentially accelerating inference. Its effectiveness depends on how much rank each matrix retains. Giving similarly sized matrices the same rank ignores differences in their effect on model quality, while optimizing ranks through repeated preliminary truncations can be expensive.

Zero Sum SVD selects singular components across the whole model. It uses activation whitening and first-order estimates of calibration-loss changes to assess components in the transformed coordinates. Its zero-sum rule keeps the cumulative predicted loss change near zero, automatically producing different ranks for different matrices without a separate rank-allocation optimization.

The method also offers a lightweight correction: one projected gradient update after compression, followed by another truncation. This is motivated by evidence of low-rank gradient structure near pretrained solutions. Experiments across multiple architectures, benchmarks, and compression ratios show consistent gains. The approach makes global loss sensitivity the organizing principle for deciding which components to retain.
icml-2026-zero-sum-svd-balancing-loss-se.tldr: Zero Sum SVD allocates compression globally by balancing predicted loss changes across singular components.
